slides.narration: Welcome. Today we study A Question of Trust by Victor Canning, the story of a careful, respectable thief who is outwitted by someone just like himself. Please read the story in your textbook, Footprints without Feet, before you go on. This lesson does not repeat the text. The board tests this reader through short and long answers, so that is our focus.

Use these slides for the sequence of events, the themes and Horace’s character.
The board asks 3-mark and 6-mark questions on this reader, not extracts: practise those most.
Explain events **in your own words**; do not memorise lines.

The board does not print extracts from this reader; it asks short and long answers. So practise explaining, in your own words, how Horace is tricked and why the ending is ironic.

slides.narration: Victor Canning, who lived from nineteen eleven to nineteen eighty-six, was an English writer of thrillers and spy novels, famous for clever plots. This short crime story is told in the third person. It is set in an English country house called Shotover Grange, and it ends with a twist that turns the whole story into an ironic lesson.

slides.heading: The story in six stages
slides.body_md: A careful thief, a careless moment. (A SOYL summary, not the text.)

visual.alt: Flow of the story in six stages: a respectable thief; the plan for Shotover Grange; inside the house; a lady in the doorway; the safe opened; prison and the truth.
visual.caption: The story in six stages (SOYL summary).

slides.narration: The story moves through six stages. We meet a respectable thief. He plans to rob Shotover Grange. He gets inside the house. A young lady appears in the doorway. He opens the safe for her. And finally, in prison, he learns the truth. Keep this map in mind as we go through each stage.

slides.heading: Summary 1: a respectable thief
slides.body_md: Horace Danby is a middle-aged, unmarried locksmith whom everyone thinks respectable. He loves rare, expensive books, and to pay for them he carries out one carefully planned robbery each year, without violence.
slides.narration: Horace Danby seems the most respectable of men. He is a middle-aged, unmarried locksmith, polite and tidy. But he has a secret. He loves rare and expensive books, and to afford them he carries out one carefully planned robbery each year. He never uses violence, and he thinks of himself almost as a gentleman. That self-image is about to be tested.

slides.heading: Summary 2: the plan for Shotover Grange
slides.body_md: This year’s target is Shotover Grange, a country house with a safe full of jewels. Horace knows the family is away in London and the servants are out. His only weakness is hay fever, and the house is full of flowers.
slides.narration: This year Horace has chosen Shotover Grange, a large country house with a safe full of valuable jewels. He has studied it carefully. The owners are away in London and the servants are out, so the house should be empty. There is one weakness he cannot plan away: he suffers from hay fever, and the rooms are full of flowers.

slides.heading: Check: the order of events
slides.narration: Your turn. Six events from the story are shuffled. Put them in order, from Horace choosing his target to his arrest.

slides.heading: Summary 3: a lady in the doorway
slides.body_md: As Horace starts work, a young woman appears, calm and amused, and lets him believe she owns the house. She says she has forgotten the safe’s combination: if he opens it for her, she will not call the police. Horace agrees.
slides.narration: Just as Horace begins, a young woman appears in the doorway. She is calm, even amused, and she lets him believe she is the lady of the house. She makes an offer. She says she has forgotten the combination of the safe; if he opens it for her, she will not call the police. Relieved and embarrassed, Horace agrees.

slides.heading: Summary 4: the safe opened
slides.body_md: Eager to show his skill, Horace opens the safe without his gloves and hands over the jewels. He leaves, relieved, believing he has escaped trouble.
slides.narration: Now Horace has an audience, and he cannot resist showing his skill. He works on the safe without his gloves, opens it and hands over the jewels. Then he leaves, relieved to have escaped so lightly. But the careful planner has just made the one mistake a careful thief must never make: he has left his fingerprints behind.

slides.heading: Summary 5: prison and the truth
slides.body_md: The jewels vanish. The police find Horace’s fingerprints and arrest him. The young woman was never the lady of the house; she was a thief. Horace ends up in prison, bitter that he was so easily used.
slides.narration: Soon the jewels are missing and the police find Horace’s fingerprints on the safe. He is arrested and sent to prison. Only then does he understand that the young woman was never the lady of the house. She was a thief, and she let him do the difficult work. In prison, Horace finds it hard to accept how easily he was used.

slides.heading: Theme 1: the deceiver deceived
slides.body_md: Horace is tricked in exactly the way he tricks others.
columns:
**How Horace deceives**

- a respectable face
- polite manners
- a trusted trade
- the world believes him

**How Horace is deceived**

- her respectable face
- her polite manners
- her air of owning the house
- he believes her
slides.narration: The central theme is the deceiver deceived. Horace fools the world with a respectable face, polite manners and a trusted trade. The young woman fools him in exactly the same way, with a respectable face, polite manners and an air of owning the house. In answers, set these side by side to show the irony clearly.

slides.heading: A web of themes

rows: A thief who fools the world is fooled by a thief.
Horace believes a stranger because she seems respectable.
Both thieves hide behind respectable faces.
Horace gains nothing and goes to prison.
Showing off his skill, he leaves fingerprints.
Horace thinks a polite crime is a harmless one.

visual.alt: Table of six themes with where each appears: the deceiver deceived, misplaced trust, appearance versus reality, crime does not pay, pride before a fall, and self-deception.

slides.narration: Around that centre sit other themes. Misplaced trust, since Horace believes a stranger. Appearance against reality, as both thieves hide behind respectable faces. Crime does not pay, because he gains nothing and goes to prison. Pride before a fall, when he works without gloves. And self-deception, as Horace tells himself that a polite crime is a harmless one.

slides.heading: Check: the same trap today
slides.narration: Check yourself. A man who often cheats others online trusts a polite stranger with his password and loses his savings. Whose fate in the story does this resemble?

slides.heading: Character: Horace Danby
slides.body_md: Your syllabus asks you to describe Horace’s character with evidence.

rows: An unmarried locksmith trusted by his neighbours.
Spends his loot on rare, costly books.
Plans one careful robbery a year; studies the house.
Thinks of himself almost as a gentleman thief.
Believes the woman’s claim to own the house.
Opens the safe without gloves for an admiring audience.

visual.alt: Table of Horace Danby’s traits with evidence: outwardly respectable, cultured, methodical, non-violent and polite, gullible, and vain about his skill.

slides.narration: Let us sketch Horace Danby. Outwardly he is respectable. He is cultured, with a love of rare books, and methodical, planning one robbery a year. He is polite and non-violent. But he is also gullible, believing the woman at once, and vain about his skill, which is why he opens the safe without gloves. His strengths and weaknesses together explain his fall.

slides.heading: The young woman

rows: Shows no fear on finding a burglar.
Turns his crime into her opportunity.
Acts the lady of the house perfectly.
Leaves Horace to take the blame.

visual.alt: Table of the young woman’s traits with evidence: cool and composed, cunning, convincing and ruthless.

slides.narration: The young woman is Horace’s mirror. She is cool and composed, showing no fear when she finds a burglar. She is cunning, turning his crime into her chance. She is convincing, acting the lady of the house perfectly. And she is ruthless, leaving him to take the blame. She is everything Horace thought he was, only cleverer.

slides.heading: Was Horace’s crime harmless?
columns:
**What Horace believed**

- he used no violence
- he robbed only once a year
- he was polite and careful

**What the story shows**

- theft is theft, however polite
- he betrayed his neighbours’ trust
- a polite thief ruins him in turn
slides.narration: A common long question asks whether Horace’s crimes were harmless. He believed so: no violence, only one robbery a year, perfect manners. But the story shows otherwise. Theft is theft, however politely done, and he betrayed the trust of everyone who thought him honest. Then a polite thief ruins him. Take a clear stand, with evidence.

slides.heading: Check: why Horace robbed
slides.narration: Try this assertion and reason item. Decide whether each statement is true, and then whether the reason really explains the assertion.

slides.heading: Irony and the twist
bullets: **Situational irony:** the trickster is tricked.
**Dramatic irony on re-reading:** the clues to the woman were there all along.
**A fitting twist:** the ending surprises, yet feels just.
**Irony of the title:** trust is the question, and the answer ruins Horace.
**Light, wry tone:** humour without a lecture.
slides.narration: How does Canning tell the story? Through irony. The trickster is tricked. On a second reading we notice the clues to the woman. The twist surprises us, yet feels just, because Horace is paid back in his own coin. The title itself is ironic: trust is the question, and his answer ruins him. And the tone stays light and wry.

slides.heading: Irony: SOYL’s own examples
slides.body_md: Practise spotting situational irony. These sentences are SOYL’s own, not from the story:
bullets: *The pickpocket reached home to find that his own wallet had been stolen on the bus.* — the cheat is cheated
*The fire station burned down during the fire-safety week.* — the protector fails
*The spelling champion misspelt her own name on the certificate.* — the expert slips
slides.narration: Here are three sentences of our own. A pickpocket’s own wallet is stolen: the cheat is cheated, just like Horace. A fire station burns during fire-safety week: the protector fails. A spelling champion misspells her name: the expert slips. In each, the outcome is the opposite of what we expect. Now find Canning’s irony in your textbook.

visual.caption: Key words for this story with their meanings.

slides.narration: These words will help you write about the story. Respectable means regarded as honest. A locksmith makes and repairs locks. Gullible means easily deceived. An allergy is a reaction to something like pollen. A combination is the sequence that opens a safe. Irony is an opposite outcome. An impostor pretends to be someone else, and a comeuppance is a deserved punishment.

slides.heading: Worked example: planning a 6-mark answer
slides.body_md: *Question:* *A thief cheated by another thief.* Discuss the irony.
bullets: **Stand:** the story is built on this irony.
**Points + evidence:** Horace’s respectable mask; the woman’s identical mask; his trust; the fingerprints.
**Turn:** prison for jewels he never kept.
**Value + conclusion:** those who exploit trust may find their own trust exploited.

slides.narration: Let us sum up. Horace Danby, a respectable locksmith, robs a single safe each year to buy rare books. At Shotover Grange a young woman, posing as the owner, asks him to open the safe. He does so without gloves and hands over the jewels. His fingerprints send him to prison, and she turns out to be a thief. Read the story in your textbook.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: 3-mark answers (40–50 words): point + evidence + explanation.
6-mark answers (100–120 words): stand → 3 points with evidence → value or theme → conclusion.
Facts often confused: the woman was not the owner; Horace kept none of the jewels; fingerprints, not a witness, convicted him.
For character questions, balance Horace’s strengths with the weaknesses that ruined him.
Value questions: honesty, trust, appearances, pride.
slides.narration: Exam tips. In three mark answers, give a point, evidence and a short explanation. In six mark answers, take a stand, give three supported points, and link to a value. Get the facts right: the woman was not the owner, Horace kept none of the jewels, and his fingerprints convicted him. In character answers, balance his strengths and weaknesses.

sections.heading: 2. Summary (in SOYL’s words)
sections.body_md:
**The thief.** Horace Danby, a middle-aged, unmarried locksmith, seems respectable to all. To buy rare, costly books he commits one carefully planned, non-violent robbery a year.

**The plan.** His target is Shotover Grange, which has a safe full of jewels. The owners are in London and the servants are out. His one weakness is hay fever, and the house is full of flowers.

**The woman.** A young woman appears, calm and amused, and lets him think she owns the house. She says she has forgotten the combination and will not call the police if he opens the safe.

**The safe.** Horace opens it without his gloves and hands over the jewels.

**The truth.** The police find his fingerprints and arrest him. The woman was a thief. Horace, in prison, finds it hard to accept how he was used.

sections.heading: 3. Themes and message
sections.body_md:
- **The deceiver deceived:** Horace is tricked as he tricks others.
- **Misplaced trust:** he believes a stranger who seems respectable.
- **Appearance versus reality:** both thieves wear respectable faces.
- **Crime does not pay:** he gains nothing and goes to prison.
- **Pride before a fall:** working without gloves.
- **Self-deception:** he thinks a polite crime is harmless.

**Message:** dishonesty catches up with us, and those who exploit trust may find their own trust exploited.

sections.heading: 8. Answering exam questions
sections.body_md:
**How this reader is examined:** the board sets 3-mark short answers (40–50 words; two of three) and a 6-mark long answer (100–120 words) on *Footprints without Feet*. It does not print extracts from this reader; SOYL’s commentary items are comprehension practice only.

**Short answers (3 marks):** point + evidence + explanation.

**Long answers (6 marks):** a clear stand; three points with evidence in your own words; a link to a value or theme; a one-line conclusion. Extrapolation tasks (Horace’s prison diary, the woman’s letter) must stay consistent with the story.

Re-read the story in *Footprints without Feet* before a test.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Board weight:** Footprints short answers (3 marks, 40–50 words, two of three) and one long answer (6 marks, 100–120 words) (CBSE 2026-27, Section C). No extracts from this reader.

**How marks are awarded:** content (relevant events, accurately used), interpretation (a clear, supported view or value), and expression within the word limit.

**Common mistakes**
1. Saying the woman owned the house: she was a thief posing as the owner.
2. Saying Horace kept the jewels: he handed them over.
3. Forgetting the gloves: his fingerprints convicted him.
4. Calling Horace violent: he prided himself on avoiding violence.
5. Quoting lines from memory instead of explaining in your own words.

**Remember:** read the story in your textbook, *Footprints without Feet*.

questions.passage_md: Canning's hero is an unusual criminal. Horace Danby is a middle-aged, unmarried man who makes locks for a living and is regarded by his neighbours as thoroughly respectable. His one passion is collecting rare, costly books, and to pay for them he commits a single, carefully planned robbery each year. He thinks of himself almost as a gentleman: polite, tidy and opposed to violence. Yet the comfortable picture hides a contradiction. A man who earns trust by making locks also earns his luxuries by breaking them, and the story will test whether such a man can himself be fooled.

answer.model_answer_md:
Prison library, evening

I still cannot believe how foolish I was. For years I planned every job with care, and nobody suspected the quiet locksmith with his rare books. At Shotover Grange everything seemed perfect: the family away, the servants out. Then that young woman appeared, so calm and elegant that I never doubted she owned the house. When she asked me to open the safe, I was flattered and relieved. I even took off my gloves to work faster. She walked away with the jewels; I walked into prison. I deceived others for years, and one clever smile deceived me. Perhaps this is the justice I always managed to avoid.

answer.model_answer_md:
Dear Kate,

You will never guess what happened at Shotover Grange. I had heard the family was away, so I slipped in to look at the safe, and found a burglar already there! He was a polite, middle-aged man, sneezing at the flowers. I pretended to be the lady of the house and said I had forgotten the combination. The poor man was so relieved not to be reported that he opened the safe for me, and without gloves too. I took the jewels, thanked him sweetly and let him go. By now the police will have found his fingerprints. Sometimes the best way to open a lock is to find someone who trusts you.

Love,
J.

answer.model_answer_md: The title is highly appropriate because trust drives every turn of the story. Horace has built a respectable life on the trust of others, who never suspect the locksmith of robbing safes. The central question arises at Shotover Grange: should he trust the young woman who catches him? He decides to believe her, because she looks and behaves like the owner, and that decision ruins him.
